channel.title: Worldview Weekly
channel.description: A weekly global counterweight reading feed: concise, analytical, low-noise, and deliberately broader in perspective than The Economist.

item.title: The ‘Stability-Instability Paradox’ Comes for Markets — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 27, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue that global energy markets’ resilience during the Iran war may itself encourage dangerous complacency. Oil shocks have been cushioned by inventories, rerouted supply and policy buffers, but those buffers are thinning. The article connects geopolitical escalation to inflation, investment signals and the limits of market adaptation.

Counterweight: Treats markets not as self-correcting abstractions but as institutions operating under geopolitical uncertainty, where successful adaptation can perversely increase risk-taking.

item.title: Ditching Chinese Rare Earths Is Hard. Just Ask Japan. — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 24, 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

Christina Lu uses Japan’s long effort to diversify away from Chinese rare earths as a warning for Washington. Even after years of stockpiling, overseas investment and alternative-supply projects, Japanese firms remain exposed to China in key heavy rare earths.

Counterweight: Complicates simple reshoring and de-risking narratives by emphasizing industrial lead times, chemistry, financing and entrenched supply chains.

item.title: Iran’s Economy May Outlast Trump’s Presidency — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 25, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Hadi Kahalzadeh argues that severe sanctions and wartime pressure may still fail to produce rapid Iranian economic collapse. Informal trade, adaptation, state controls and long experience with sanctions give Tehran more resilience than headline indicators imply.

Counterweight: Challenges the assumption that economic pressure mechanically converts into political capitulation.

item.title: Who Reaps the Benefits of India’s Growth? — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 21, 2026 · medium-long (~18 min)

Sumit Ganguly reviews a major new account of India’s development trajectory, focusing on how early policy choices shaped today’s combination of rapid growth, weak job creation and persistent inequality.

Counterweight: Keeps business and development in the same frame: high headline growth is not enough if productive employment and broad-based capability formation lag behind.

item.title: Peacemaking Is Power Politics Again — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 25, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Comfort Ero and Richard Gowan argue that the post-Cold War model of institutionalized peacemaking has weakened as major powers return to bargaining, coercion and ad hoc diplomacy. Conflict mediation is migrating toward regional powers and influential capitals rather than disappearing.

Counterweight: Avoids both nostalgia for the old multilateral order and fatalism about its decline.

item.title: Is Europe Ready for a New Era of Russian Dirty Tricks? — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 26, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Christian Caryl examines Russia’s increasing use of sabotage, covert action, drones and other gray-zone tactics against Europe. The challenge is not simply military deterrence but institutional resilience against ambiguous attacks below the threshold of war.

Counterweight: Shifts attention from conventional force balances toward infrastructure protection and the politics of attribution.

item.title: The U.S. Is Learning the Wrong Lessons in Iran — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 21, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Bret Devereaux argues that debates over logistics, drones and munitions risk missing the deeper lesson of the Iran war: tactical excellence cannot rescue incoherent strategy.

Counterweight: Pushes against technocratic “lessons learned” analysis that treats war chiefly as a procurement and operational-efficiency problem rather than a political one.

item.title: The U.S. Can’t Catch Up to China’s Robots by Banning Them — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 25, 2026 · medium (~12 min)

James Palmer argues that China’s strength in robotics comes from industrial depth, manufacturing scale and iterative deployment—not merely access to individual technologies.

Counterweight: Treats technology competition as an industrial-development problem rather than a sanctions problem.

item.title: Stumped by a Medical Mystery? Try Metagenomics — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 25, 2026 · medium-long (~20 min)

Jason Liebowitz explores metagenomic sequencing as a diagnostic tool for mysterious infections: instead of testing for one suspected pathogen at a time, clinicians search broadly for genetic fragments from viruses, bacteria and fungi.

Counterweight: Shows innovation as an institutional process of validation and interpretation, not merely a breakthrough waiting to diffuse.

item.title: How the Job Market Will Shape the Next Generation — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 25, 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

Jay Caspian Kang looks at how a difficult early-career labor market may shape the political and social outlook of younger workers. Prolonged difficulty entering stable careers can change attitudes toward institutions, risk and the social contract.

Counterweight: Connects labor-market statistics to generational politics and identity.

item.title: Should You Believe in Fate? — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 21, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Joshua Rothman considers why ideas of fate remain psychologically attractive in societies that prize agency and optimization, and whether meaning may come partly from accepting the physical and social world around us.

Counterweight: Gives the issue a deliberately non-instrumental cultural perspective.

item.title: The End of the European Summer — The New Yorker
item.description:
WORLDVIEW BACKGROUND · The New Yorker · August 24 & 31 issue · long (~30–35 min)

Eric Klinenberg reports on how European cities are redesigning streets, public space, shade, vegetation and cooling systems as extreme heat becomes a structural urban problem. The article is slightly outside this week’s publication window, but its importance and breadth justify carrying it forward.

Why it pierces through: It turns climate adaptation into a concrete question of urban design, public goods and inequality.
